claim.precise: The Passover rite narrated and explained in Exodus 12:21–27 is fulfilled typologically in Christ, whom Paul explicitly calls ‘our Passover lamb’ in 1 Corinthians 5:7.
claim.scope_notes: Grant Paul's explicit identification and evaluate whether it proves a prospective Exodus prediction, rather than confusing a strong NT typology with a direct oracle.

context.summary: Exodus 12:21–27 directs Israelite households to slaughter the Passover animal, put its blood on doorframes, stay inside until morning, and explain to later children that God spared their Egyptian homes. In 1 Corinthians 5:6–8 Paul applies the Passover and unleavened-bread feast to a church facing an ethical problem, saying Christ the Passover has been sacrificed and urging sincerity rather than malice.

strongest_case.summary: 1 Corinthians 5:7 directly identifies Christ as ‘our Passover’ and says he has been sacrificed; BSB supplies ‘lamb’ to express the ritual referent. Paul's following verse asks Christians to keep the feast ethically, making the typology sustained, not an incidental image. Jamieson–Fausset–Brown explicitly links 5:7 to Exodus 12:5–11 and 21–23. The strongest Christian reading says the Exodus rescue ritual becomes an intentional template for Christ's sacrificial work and the community's new life.
reasoning: Paul directly names Christ as Passover rather than relying on a loose allusion.
Passover and unleavened-bread imagery extends across 1 Corinthians 5:6–8.
A named Christian commentary documents the Exodus–Paul linkage.

critical_case.summary: Exodus 12:21–27 gives Israel instructions for a historical deliverance and a continuing family memorial, explicitly interpreting the rite as God's sparing of Israelite homes in Egypt. It does not describe or date a future Messiah's death. Paul's reinterpretation is deliberate and substantial, but it is a later christological use of an earlier ritual. Moreover, 1 Corinthians 5:7 belongs to an argument about removing corrupting ‘leaven’ from the Corinthian church, not to an evidentiary demonstration that Exodus originally predicted Jesus.
reasoning: Exodus itself supplies the first rite's meaning to later children.
Paul uses Passover as both sacrificial identification and an ethical exhortation.
A later typological application need not be a prior, testable prediction.

textual_issues.issue: No material variant drives the conclusion. In 1 Corinthians 5:7 Paul explicitly says Christ is ‘our Passover’ (to pascha hēmōn); BSB's ‘lamb’ makes the sacrificial referent explicit in English, but the identification survives without that supplied noun. The dispute is interpretive classification, not whether Paul made the connection.

verdict.summary: Paul explicitly and meaningfully treats Christ as Passover, so the Christian typology is well evidenced. Exodus 12:21–27 explained an Egyptian deliverance and prescribed a continuing memorial; it did not prospectively predict Jesus. The claim succeeds as NT typology, not as a distinctive prior prophecy.

objections.objection: Christian defenders may count divinely intended Passover typology as fulfilment without requiring a verbal forecast.
objections.reason: The article explicitly grants Paul's intentional and strong typological fulfilment; it limits only the original-text prediction claim.

objections.objection: Broader Passover details and other NT parallels could strengthen the case.
objections.reason: The checked Exodus 12 context and JFB source support the wider rite; this claim is still evaluated individually against 12:21–27 and 1 Corinthians 5:7, whose explicit connection is sufficient.

objections.objection: ‘Reinterpretation’ may imply distortion where Paul may make a legitimate christological application.
objections.reason: The resolution uses neutral language of intentional typological application and does not rule out theological intention.

objections.objection: BSB's ‘Passover lamb’ may supply the noun ‘lamb’ rather than quote Paul's exact Greek wording.
objections.reason: The textual issue now distinguishes Paul's explicit ‘our Passover’ from the English gloss; the core identification remains clear.

publication_copy.title: Christ, our Passover
publication_copy.scripture_excerpt: It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck down the Egyptians and spared our homes.

website.description: Paul calls Christ the Passover lamb. Does Exodus 12 predict him?
website.summary: Paul explicitly calls Christ ‘our Passover lamb.’ That is a strong Christian link—but what kind?
website.christian_case: 1 Corinthians 5:7 directly identifies Christ as the sacrificed Passover lamb. Paul carries the feast image into verse 8, asking the church to live with sincerity instead of malice. Christians are not inventing the link after the fact; a New Testament writer makes it deliberately.
website.critical_case: Exodus 12 itself explains Passover as a memory of homes spared in Egypt and commands Israel to repeat the rite. It does not forecast a particular future death. Paul applies the older ritual to Jesus and his church's conduct, which is typology rather than a prior prediction.
website.verdict: The Passover–Christ connection is strongly supported as Paul's own theological reading. It does not show that Exodus 12:21–27 originally predicted Jesus.

carousel.heading: Paul makes the link explicit
carousel.body: Exodus describes the Passover sacrifice that spared Israelite homes in Egypt. Paul writes, ‘Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.’ This is a direct Christian identification.
carousel.alt_text: Slide 1: Exodus Passover and Paul's explicit statement.

carousel.heading: More than a loose resemblance
carousel.body: Paul continues the feast image in 1 Corinthians 5:8, urging his church to live without the ‘leaven’ of malice. His reading intentionally connects Christ's sacrifice and a new way of life.
carousel.alt_text: Slide 2: The strongest Christian Passover typology.

carousel.heading: The earlier rite had its own meaning
carousel.body: Exodus says the rite remembers God's rescue of homes in Egypt and tells children to keep explaining it. Paul applies that history to Christ later. Strong typology does not turn the rite into a prior prediction.
carousel.alt_text: Slide 3: An explicit NT connection is not an original Exodus prophecy.
